items.body:
In **[Part 1](https://mbideepdives.substack.com/p/modeling-alphabet-part-1-search-gemini)** yesterday, I went through the Google Services segment, especially its “problem child”: Search. Today is about the business that may be Alphabet’s new crown jewel, Google Cloud, along with the cost of training Gemini, capex and what all of it means for the stock. I will also explore what the post-Jensen question may mean for Alphabet.

_Subscribers get the daily journal and five+ years of Deep Dives, i.e. full-length analyses with financial models on **[70](https://mbideepdives.substack.com/p/deep-dives)+** companies. The daily is just how I think out loud between the Deep Dives!_

items.title: Conditions for agentic commerce
items.body: Third-party agentic commerce viability depends on fulfillment structures, advertising risks, and consumer preference clarity. While dominant platforms resist agents to protect advertising revenue and direct relationships, categories like travel and SaaS offer better integration opportunities. Success requires incentive alignment between agents, retailers, and consumer welfare regarding price and delivery.

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.body: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models , where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic , launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it! ” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Why Cloudflare is in the lab now Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models. “Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,” Chen said in her presentation. In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations. “I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space , because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.” If you look at Cloudflare’s product page now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there! But there’s still room for several more models.

items.title: 💰 Wall Street's Top Stocks in Q3
items.body: Welcome to the Premium edition of How They Make Money . Over 300,000 subscribers turn to us for business and investment insights. In case you missed it: 📊 Earnings Visuals (10/2026) 🤖 How Anthropic Makes Money 💻 PRO: Microsoft Azure Hits 48% 🚨 NVIDIA: Jensen Huang Resigns Subscribe now It’s 13F season again! Every quarter, funds managing over $100 million must disclose their portfolios, offering a rare glimpse into the minds of elite investors. The latest 13F filings capture portfolios as of September 30. Of course, a lot has happened since then. At the end of Q3, the AI infrastructure boom was still in full swing. Hyperscalers were pouring billions into data centers, semiconductor stocks were riding a wave of demand, and investors were looking for the next beneficiaries across the supply chain. Fast-forward six weeks, and the picture looks very different. The Democrats swept the midterm elections, voters pushed back against new data centers, and NVIDIA lost its longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, in a stunning leadership shakeup. Meanwhile, the AI trade has suffered a sharp selloff. Concerns about circular financing, the returns on massive AI investments, and persistently high inflation have weighed on valuations. So where were the world’s leading investors putting their money before the turmoil? Were they still piling into AI infrastructure, taking profits, or finding opportunities elsewhere? Let’s find out. Today at a glance: Hedge funds’ strategies Top buys and top holdings in Q3 Fund picks that were not on your bingo card Implications for individual investors 📊 Black Friday: PRO is 40% off for life Get our weekly PRO coverage of the biggest market leaders, with timely earnings breakdowns, KPI tracking, and visuals that help connect the dots. For Black Friday, unlock PRO at $299/year instead of $499/year, and keep that price for as long as your subscription remains active. But don’t wait! The offer ends on Sunday. Go PRO 40% Off Before we dive into 13Fs, a quick reminder: blindly copying hedge fund trades is a terrible strategy. Investing is like shooting 3-pointers. Even Steph Curry, the greatest shooter ever, misses more than half the time. No outcomes are guaranteed, even for the pros. Your behavior matters more than your portfolio. As Peter Lynch said, “Know what you own and why you own it.” Conviction is what helps you hold through volatility. And conviction comes from doing your own work, not borrowing someone else’s. As Ian Cassel puts it: “You can borrow someone else’s stock ideas but you can’t borrow their conviction. […] Do the work so you know when to sell. Do the work so you can hold. Do the work so you can stand alone.” Some limitations of 13F filings: Omit short positions and cash reserves. Offer a partial view , leaving out smaller funds. Exclude many non-US equities , bonds, and commodities. Can be dated , as filings are due up to 45 days after quarter-end. With all this said, let’s see what top funds were buying and holding in Q3. 1. Hedge funds’ strategies Hedge funds are financial powerhouses known for flexible, aggressive strategies designed to beat the market. Here’s what typically shapes their moves: Market conditions : Long in bull markets, defensive in bear markets. Sector trends : Shifts in regulation or consumer behavior steer capital. Fundamentals : Strong earnings, free cash flow, and leadership matter. Macro factors : Rates, inflation, and geopolitics influence positioning. Quant models : Some lean on proprietary algorithms to find an edge. Risk management : Diversification, hedging, and position sizing. Investor sentiment : Fear and greed create mispriced opportunities. Still, it doesn’t always work out. The Global X Guru ETF (GURU), designed to track top hedge fund holdings, has underperformed the S&P 500 since its inception in 2012. And that comparison still leaves out the classic hedge fund fee drag. Source: Fiscal.ai And those fees matter. The classic “2 and 20” model (2% of assets + 20% of gains) can significantly reduce returns. It’s no wonder that many individual investors are opting for simpler, lower-cost strategies. 2. Top holdings and top buys in Q3 Our partners at Fiscal.ai gather the data on Super Investors and visualize their portfolios for you. Pick your favorite investors and see how their holdings have evolved. Source: Fiscal.ai In early 2020, just before the COVID market turmoil, I curated a list of 20 top-performing hedge funds using TipRanks data. The selection focused on alpha relative to the S&P 500, and I also included a few funds frequently featured in my social feeds and podcast rotation. It’s not perfect, but it remains a solid directional filter. Top 5 holdings at the end of September 2026: The 10 stocks below represent nearly half of the top holdings listed: ☁️ Hyperscalers: AMZN, META, GOOG, MSFT. 🤖 AI infrastructure: TSM, NVDA, MU, LRCX. 🚀 Recent IPOs: SPCX, CBRS. Amazon is now the most widely held stock, appearing among the top five holdings of 11 funds, up from nine in Q2. Taiwan Semiconductor follows with nine, unchanged from last quarter. Meta saw the biggest jump, rising from three to nine appearances. Microsoft also gained ground, moving from one to three. Meanwhile, Alphabet fell from eight to four, while NVIDIA held steady at five. Apple remains absent from the top-five holdings, while Tesla appears at Altimeter. Of course, these rankings reflect both portfolio decisions and stock-price movements. A company dropping out of a fund’s top five doesn’t necessarily mean the manager sold shares. The holdings don’t change dramatically from quarter to quarter, so let’s turn to the more actionable insights in the new Q3 movements. Top 5 buys in Q3 Read more

items.title: [AINews] Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026
items.body: Perplexity crossed a $1B annual revenue run rate today , CEO Aravind Srinivas told Semafor at a live event. The Information reported previously under $250M at the start of the year and over $750M by August, with Computer driving some of the growth. At usual agent lab multiples (eg Cognition also crossed $1B , with Cursor crossing $4.6B ), this would roughly mean that Perplexity is now worth $30-50B — if the unit economics hold up. This is a nice bump on the $20B round in September 2025 , and qualifies for our “>$10B fundraise” rule for title stories. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Watch a topic or page and get a webhook when something relevant changes. Frontier Research. The new research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code. Sponsored by Deepgram Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI. For any stack and any tools you already love building with, Deepgram slots in as your foundational voice AI technology. So you have control. And we have the context to listen, understand, and speak like a human. Learn more about the Real-time Context Standard . AI Twitter Recap Qwen4-Max in the wild Friday’s Qwen4-Max preview is now a shipping model. At the highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scored 43 on the Intelligence Index, up from 34. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial Analysis Inside the model. Alibaba kept the total parameter count at 2.4T and reduced the number active per token by 25% to 71B. The model takes images and text, with a 1M-token context window. Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are still to come. Alibaba Arena and Vals : Arena ranks it #14 overall on Agent Arena, the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions ( Arena ). WebDev : It placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, +74 over its predecessor ( WebDev ). It also placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol ( I2WebDev ). Vals Index : It is #11 overall, with large gains in coding and finance ( Vals ). Legal-benchmark caveat : On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x ( HLAB ). Vision results (independent) : Roboflow calls it underwhelming on its VLM benchmark, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic now far ahead. At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max ( Roboflow ). Safety, alignment and eval integrity OpenAI embedded assessments : OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems ( OpenAI ). Scope by group : Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months ( Rundown ). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots ( METR ). Transluce runs a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027 ( Transluce ). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs ( Goodfire ). Limits : METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed ( scope ). Criticism of the access terms : Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps : Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation ( Neel Nanda , Alex Mallen ). Former-employee account : Mikita Balesni says assessors cannot quote employees, even anonymously, and some may be barred from publishing on internal-only models ( balesni ). Goodfire acquisition talks : The Information reports OpenAI explored buying the interpretability startup for more than $5B. Goodfire reportedly wanted to stay independent so it could sell to multiple labs ( report ). Other integrity signals : Benchmark contamination : Claude appears to have memorized details of the LinuxArena control eval ( Karvonen ). Incident taxonomy : OpenAI published a v0.1 framework for classifying AI control incidents ( framework ). Disclosure policy : Anthropic is cutting its coordinated disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities ( policy ). Inference systems and agent infrastructure Together moves on from hand-tuned megakernels. Its first design made it into production for one customer. Agents now search for smaller groups of GPU operations to fuse. Together reports 28% higher throughput on Llama 3.2 1B on B200. Engineering writeup DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Vera Rubin : vLLM with Dynamo on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark shows 63.4x per-chip throughput over GB300 NVL72 at 400 tok/s/user, and 93.3x at 600 ( vLLM ). Batch-1 latency : SGLang-adjacent work reaches ~2,500 tok/s at batch size 1 on TP4, 1.7x its GB300 result ( saltyph ). Baseten reports a similar 1.7x over its 4xB300 numbers ( Baseten ). Agent-driven optimization : An agent shared Engram tables across HBM via NVLink symmetric memory to recover prefix-cache capacity ( Liu ). Another team says agents found optimizations that made its B300 step time 10% faster ( Halex ). Agentic serving research : MIT's Evolving Infra replaces fixed prefill/decode disaggregation with online adaptation. Against NVIDIA Dynamo on up to 256 GB300s, it reports up to 4.1x lower latency and 14x lower P95 TTFT ( Evolving Infra ). Pipeline-parallel prefill : Inferact finds PP2 on MiniMax-M3.1-Flash sustains 23% more requests per GPU than DEP2 at a 2s TTFT target ( Inferact ). Prefix-cache pitfalls : Ollama found that a single system-prompt timestamp or a change in reasoning effort can wipe the cache ( Ollama ). Sandboxes and training : External sandboxes : Simon Willison describes running agents on a Mac while executing their code in WebAssembly, QEMU or Apple Container sandboxes. The pattern includes allow-list proxies and credential replacement ( post ). MLPerf : In MLPerf Training v6.1, a GB300 NVL72 trained GPT-OSS-20B in 19.7 minutes, 2.86x faster than H100 ( Lambda ). One endpoint for open models. Hugging Face Inference Providers now runs on OpenRouter using the same endpoint and token. Hugging Face Research, benchmarks and evals PyBot : A swarm of 1,000 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash agents spent a week writing a rule-based chatbot with no neural network ( lewtun ). Scale : The agents exchanged ~175k messages and merged ~8k PRs. Result : The bot is 630k lines of Python with zero dependencies and is reported on par with SmolLM-360M on everyday questions. Self-improvement and training : AutoRL : Agents supervising a live RL run lifted Qwen3 on AIME 2024 from 46.67% to 66.67% ( omarsar0 ). Benchmark-gaming caveat : A roundup warns that many self-improving agent gains come from learning the benchmark rather than the task ( TuringPost ). Weight-space programming : Opus 5.5 hand-wrote transformer weights that solved algorithmic tasks with a median of 166 parameters ( dair_ai ). Data curation : DatologyAI published the tech report behind its claimed 6x pretraining compute multiplier ( Datology ). Distillation reproduction : A small-scale replication confirms perturbed-input distillation helps when the student trains from scratch, but finds it hurts when distilling into a pretrained student ( Maini ). New benchmarks : GradeBench : The best frontier model agrees with instructors only 57% of the time when grading handwritten physics answers ( GradeBench ). Time to First Audio : AA's new TTS latency benchmark finds a median of 376 ms for streaming models versus 2.0 s for non-streaming ones ( AA ). SpeedRunBench : Inkling-2-Small cleared SuperTux 1-1 in 1,988 frames, ahead of Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol ( SpeedRunBench ). Science models and developer tools Gemini 4 Carbon : DeepMind says Carbon powered AlphaProof Code agents that verified Signal's cryptographic code. It also spotted wet-lab errors and found 40x more related protein sequences ( details ). Science access : Google expanded free Carbon access for 10,000 scientists through Antigravity ( program ). Context window : Antigravity doubled the context window for Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen, cutting compaction 3.5x per user turn ( Mohan ). User reports (anecdotal) : One researcher says Carbon solved a problem that waves of Astra and Fable attempts had not ( anecdote ). OpenAI for science and health : OpenAI is opening free frontier access to up to 200,000 scientists, with applications from Nov 23 ( program ). Productivity study : OpenAI reports scientists roughly doubled their productivity in a study of 1,800 participants ( study ). Physics showcase : Physicist Nathaniel Craig used GPT-6 Astra to develop a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model ( blog ). Healthcare : ChatGPT for Healthcare adds computer-use agents and more than 20 plugins ( healthcare ). Claude Code : The desktop app now runs iPhone Duo in the iOS simulator and can fold and unfold the device to test layouts ( ClaudeDevs ). Verification : The team published how it uses cheap tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs to let Claude verify its own work ( blog ). Unreleased model (unconfirmed) : A "Silicon 2" entry spotted in Devin is suspected to be an Anthropic model ( rumor ). Liquid d1.2-ultra : It ranks #1 on AA's Decision Index at $0.042 per M input tokens ( AA ). Sage S2.1 Flash : The open-weight science model reports leading MLE-bench Lite and OfficeQA Pro results ( Sage ). FLUX-mimic-x : A 7B video-action robotics model ranks #1 on RoboLab among real-time models ( mimic ). Unsloth computer use : Local models can now drive desktop apps and game engines through Unsloth ( Unsloth ). Industry and policy Nvidia. The US Commerce and Justice departments issued a joint statement on the Megaspeed investigation. Commerce Financing and M&A : Noeri : Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin's continual-learning lab raised $110M ( Choi ). Corma : The cyber-defense model company raised a $125M Series A at a $1B valuation ( Corma ). World Labs : The team is joining AMD ( Fei-Fei Li ). Market data : Anthropic's S-1 shows $16.3B revenue in H1 2026 and compute costs falling from 251% to 48% of revenue ( The Batch ). Enterprise adoption : Databricks reports open-model token share rose from 7.3% to 30.9% in 3.5 months ( summary ). AI Reddit Recap Local models and hardware What fits in 16 GB? Unsloth expects a smaller Qwen4-27B to run in 16 GB. Local users want to see the quantization and how much memory is left for the context window. One developer already splits coding jobs between Opus for specs and a local Qwen3.8-27B for implementation. Memory discussion · Local workflows Hy4 Flash. Tencent’s multimodal model has 224B parameters and activates 12B per token. At $0.070 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens, it gives developers a cheaper way to try Hy4’s 1M context window. Tencent’s release · Discussion EUROPA. A reported test run on the JUPITER supercomputer trained a roughly 952B-parameter mixture of experts with 32.8B parameters active per token. The local-model community’s question is why the team chose that scale for its first model. Training run and discussion Where do two quantizations diverge? inside-llm loads two GGUFs with the same tokenizer and lets you step through their predictions side by side. Watch the first token where they disagree, then compare the probabilities they assigned to the alternatives. Project · Demo and discussion Basalt’s 770 tokens/sec headline depends on what you generate. The developer reports up to 776 tokens/sec for structured output from Qwen3.8-27B, 262 in chat and 194 for prose. Readers asked for longer quality tests of the 4-bit prefill. Basalt · Benchmark thread An FPGA running Qwen 27B. Valley Semiconductor reports 7.9 tokens/sec on short prompts and about 5.5 in live chat. Its 50 tokens/sec target at 20 W is a projection for a future chip. Live demo · Hardware discussion Agents in use Claude Meetings. A CTO describes inviting Claude into a 30-minute Google Meet. It updated project records in Notion and called the team’s own tools to update bids during the meeting. Field report A Minecraft test for Hydrogen. A developer asked Gemini 4 Hydrogen to recover missing source and build a datapack for 11 Minecraft versions. The agent reportedly launched two graphical clients to test fixes for dropped items and raycasts. Developer’s account What teams hire a harness developer to do. One example from the discussion: a coding agent can propose a change, while the harness decides which repository it may write to, which CI test counts as passing and when a person needs to approve the next step. Claude Code discussion Vision and video Testing a video model’s physics. After a second MiniMax H3 demo, commenters proposed a harder test: describe the scene, leave the outcome out of the prompt and see whether the model predicts what the objects will do. Demo and discussion

Every single one explained as a “technical issue.” Every single one unrelated. Sure. Maybe it really is coincidence, aging infrastructure, bad luck in a cluster. But somebody bought a lot of crash insurance right before the dominoes started tipping.

items.body: https://t.co/DrLGfxIj3m GAI DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT DAILY DIGEST, MONDAY, NOVEMBER 16, 2026 LEAD ITEMS - TIZA AI Gebeng AI Data Centre Park, Kuantan, Pahang, Malaysia: first public surfacing of a named AI data centre park whose government task force approval carries up to 1,300 MW of electricity demand to be met off-grid; the 11/16/26 MoU is a feasibility framework only, detailed under NEW LAUNCHES. NEW LAUNCHES - TIZA AI Gebeng AI Data Centre Park, Kuantan, Pahang, Malaysia, event 11/16/26, verified. Citaglobal (via Citaglobal New Energy), TNB GENCO and TIZA AI signed an MoU to develop a dedicated off-grid power supply for TIZA AI's proposed AI Data Centres & Digital Infrastructure Park on Citaglobal's 247-acre Gebeng Industrial Area site. TIZA AI holds the Data Centre Task Force approval (notified 09/07/26) requiring the park's demand of up to 1,300 MW to be met off-grid. The 1,300 MW is an approved maximum demand figure, not committed IT capacity; no phase MW, tenant, timeline or investment was disclosed, and the one-year MoU commits no party to build, supply or purchase. No pin verified. - Enlight Shemen Hof Shemen Data Center, Haifa, Israel, event 11/16/26, verified. Enlight Renewable Energy and Shemen Yielding Real Estate will develop, finance, construct and operate a data center of up to 150 MW planned power capacity at Hof Shemen, Haifa, through a 50/50 project company under a lease of about 25 years. A 150 MW grid connection application has been submitted and its documentation confirmed complete; advancement is gated by the Electricity Authority's final decision, carried under REGULATORY RESTRICTIONS. The 150 MW is an up-to planning figure, not a committed build figure. No pin verified. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the Google Ozans campus at Etrechet, France (verified 11/13/26 as a consultation capture); tonight's new Ozans event, the ENGIE energy partnership MoU of 11/13/26, is carried under PROJECT EVOLUTIONS. PROJECT EVOLUTIONS - ENGIE and Google Ozans partnership, Etrechet, France, LATE, event 11/13/26, verified. ENGIE signed an MoU to become the preferred energy supplier and management partner for Google's Ozans campus, subject to further agreements. The campus record stands: about 195 hectares, phase 1 of 120 MW on a 225 kV RTE connection with a first building around 2030, and the CNDP public consultation running to 01/10/27. - Core Scientific Hunt County Campus, Quinlan, Texas, event 11/16/26, corroborated. Telios Quinlan One filed with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation for a 341,325 sq ft core and shell building, $1.3 billion, construction 11/16/26 to 09/30/28, the campus's first filed construction window (up to 285 MW leasable, 430 MW gross). The filing is follow-up evidence against the satellite STALLED watch on this campus: forward motion on paper, site activity not yet confirmed. Site-work pass, permit-in direction. - Soluna Project Kati 2, Willacy County, Texas, LATE, November 2026 (month precision), confirmed. Pre-lease: after the prior prospective tenant's exclusivity ended, Soluna signed a non-binding LOI with a new prospective tenant to lease 118 IT MW at the planned 350+ MW Kati 2 campus. Tenant unnamed, term not published. Pre-leasing pass item. - Soluna Kati 2 and Dorothy 3, Texas, LATE, October 2026 (month precision), corroborated. Construction began at both Kati 2 and Dorothy 3 in October, per Soluna's Q3 release and 10-Q filed today; Kati 1 completed its final 14 MW on 09/08/26 and is fully energized at 83 MW. - Early-works award: TeraWulf Justified Data Campus, Hawesville, Kentucky, LATE, event 11/04/26, corroborated. Fluor's March limited notice to proceed converted to a definitive EPC contract for three buildings, and Fluor states early works construction has already begun. Phased ready-for-service completions run late 2027 through Q2 2028; the $4 billion figure in reporting is the campus cost, not the EPC value. Site-work pass, contractor-out direction. New campus record, no pin verified. - QTS Proyecto Rhodes Campus, Calatorao, Aragon, Spain, event 11/16/26, single-source. DCD, citing El Espanol, reports the Blackstone campus at 430 MW in two phases with investment above 13 billion euros, against the initial announcement of 300 MW and 7.5 billion euros, after the 150 MW Box2Bit grid connection transfer below. Whether the transferred 150 MW sits inside the 430 MW is not stated, and the census figure on file is not restated on this item. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the AWS Wheatfield (Project Rise) groundbreaking write-up (the groundbreaking stands captured with its 11/12/26 event date), and the Envision Galaxy Ulanqab 800V-live milestone, whose reports conflict at 3 GW against 800 MW by end-2027; neither figure was adopted. BLOCKERS - TELUS withdraws from Westbank 150 West Georgia AI Factory, Vancouver, Canada, LATE, event 11/15/26, corroborated. TELUS confirmed it will not co-develop the planned 10-storey, up to 100 MW AI data centre targeted online 2029. Westbank says the project proceeds under a new partnership not yet announced. TELUS gave no reason; Globe and Mail sourcing attributes the reconsideration to lack of local support, labeled single-source inside the finding. - TELUS withdraws from Westbank M3 Mount Pleasant AI Factory, Vancouver, Canada, LATE, event 11/15/26, corroborated. The same withdrawal at the M3 conversion (about 100,000 sq ft, was projected to begin operating end of 2026). The end-2026 target now rests with a developer whose operating partner has exited and is unnamed: timeline at risk, not formally slipped. A further city consultation on the M3 application runs 12/02/26 to 12/15/26. - Box2Bit Epilon Campus, Epila, Aragon, Spain, event 11/16/26, single-source. Box2Bit (Capital Energy) has withdrawn from the Epilon project and is selling its 150 MW grid connection to Blackstone, after Red Electrica denied consumption access at the Calatorao 220 kV substation, a first land payment was missed, and land rights expired in May 2026. DCD states all three of Box2Bit's announced Aragon campuses are now dead on grid access. No operator statement was retrieved tonight. REGULATORY RESTRICTIONS - Mesa County, Colorado, LATE, event 09/29/26, verified. Commissioners unanimously approved a 12-month moratorium on acceptance, processing and approval of data center land use applications in unincorporated Mesa County while the land development code is updated. The county states it has no pending data center applications. The county's own release was published today. - Israel Electricity Authority grid framework, Haifa, Israel, event 11/16/26, confirmed. The Enlight and Shemen parties state their 150 MW Hof Shemen agreement is expressly subject to the Authority's binding final decision on its proposed data center grid connection framework; the project's 150 MW application is confirmed complete. October reporting put the framework's shape at a 200 MW cap per new site with about 1,300 MW of cumulative connections allocated to the first projects approved by June 2028, single-chain context until the final text publishes. - Pitt County, North Carolina, event 11/16/26, single-source, watch. The Board of Commissioners held its public hearing tonight (6:45pm EST) on a proposed moratorium on construction and expansion of commercial data centers. Scheduling a hearing did not enact a pause; the adoption outcome was not reported by run time and is checked tomorrow. - Dedham, Massachusetts, event 11/16/26, single-source, watch. Fall Town Meeting opened tonight (7:00pm EST) with Article 8 on the warrant, a Planning Board proposal to pause data center development until 11/30/27 while an advisory committee drafts permanent zoning. No vote result was available by run time; checked tomorrow. - Salisbury, Maryland, LATE, events 09/14/26 to 11/10/26, single-source. A developer with a lease to convert a former pharmaceutical plant (about 11 MW) says the city confirmed the use was permitted in writing, then voted to freeze data center applications for a year. City records corroborate the moratorium track: a 09/14/26 work session on a one-year freeze while a zoning definition is drafted, and the definition advanced 11/10/26. - San Francisco, California, event 11/16/26, lead only. An X post reports large public-comment turnout at the Land Use Committee advocating a data center moratorium. No vote, bill text or outcome was grounded in a non-X source tonight; captured as an unverified lead and nothing more. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the Minneapolis downtown-overlay and renewable-power ordinance (captured with its 11/12/26 event date; the measure now goes to the mayor, with a council meeting 11/20/26 on a possible veto), the Oakland unanimous 10.5-month moratorium extension (verified 11/13/26), the Independence, Missouri republication of its July moratorium release (a republication, not a new event), and the Loudoun County status check: the pause vote is on tomorrow's 11/17/26 agenda as item 14.m, and that finding has moved to watch for the decision. COMMUNITY ISSUES - Sutton, Massachusetts, event 11/16/26, single-source. One week after the 900 MW, $16 billion Kraft Group (Unified Global Packaging) campus debuted, a citizens petition gathered about 300 signatures in two days, passing the requirement to force a special town meeting vote on prohibiting data centers. Once filed and certified, the town has 45 days to hold the meeting. No application has been submitted for the campus yet. - Trenton, Ohio (Prologis Project Mila), LATE, event 11/12/26, corroborated. After nearly 80 percent of voters passed Issue 17 on 11/03/26, a charter amendment banning data centers over 25 MW, Prologis sued the City of Trenton in federal court on 11/12/26 to protect approvals secured before the vote for its 141-acre, reportedly 250 MW campus, where groundworks have begun. Conserve Ohio separately threatens suit to revoke the zoning certificate. The vote is now in court from both sides. - Botetourt County, Virginia (Google Greenfield), LATE, event 11/10/26, corroborated. A judge overruled the county's and Helio Capital's demurrers and let a resident's FOIA lawsuit over the reported $3 billion Google campus performance agreement proceed; the suit asks the court to void the agreement approved in a June 2025 closed session. The main hearing was held today, 11/16/26; its outcome was not yet reported at run time and is an open follow-up. - Pennhurst, East Vincent Township, Pennsylvania, LATE, event 11/10/26, single-source. A Chester County judge granted the adjoining farm owners and East Vincent Advocacy intervenor status to defend the township's unanimous May denial of the conditional use application for the roughly 123-acre Pennhurst proposal, against the developer's appeal. The merits were not reached. - Amsterdam, Netherlands (Pure DC AMS01 for Microsoft), LATE, event 11/06/26, corroborated. Activists occupied the Pure DC construction site during the Europe-wide action days; Dutch police put the final detention count at 218, all released the next day. No project change was announced. Dutch-language searching was run before this item was recorded. - Zaragoza, Aragon, Spain, LATE, event 11/07/26, corroborated. Thousands marched demanding a moratorium on large Aragon data centers. Attendance is disputed: organizers and https://t.co/tABPjAHtfn Aragon say about 5,000, the Policia Nacional figure is about 2,000; both are carried, neither adopted. Spanish-language searching was run before recording. - Sangamon County, Illinois (CyrusOne), LATE, event 11/06/26, single-source. A circuit judge dismissed the residents' lawsuit challenging the county's conditional use approval for the CyrusOne campus before trial, holding the board's action highly presumed valid. The community's court route on this approval is closed at this level; the item resolves in the buildout's favor. - East Whiteland Township, Pennsyl

items.title: Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly
items.body: Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later. It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the photons as a pixel with a value of 0.5, so you can do the obvious linear math to calculate partial pixel coverage, blending a foreground over a background, or interpolating between colors in a texture. If displays are “linear”, that is correct. NeXT and 3DFX were much closer to linear than other contemporary displays. NeXT had crossover from the deep graphics understanding at Pixar, and 3DFX had the SGI heritage. They did this intentionally. If you have 10+ bits per channel like the professional rendering systems, linear displays are The Right Thing. Unfortunately, NeXTStation Colors were 4 bits per channel and 3DFX was 5 or 6 bits per channel, and there… it was not the right thing. Human eyes aren’t linear intensity sensors. We mostly register relative changes in intensity, so we can tell the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as a huge doubling, while 0.99 to 1.00 is almost imperceptible. This distribution of intensities is often referred to as the “gamma” of the display system, but the actual curves like sRGB are a bit more complicated. If you only have a small number of discrete pixel values, you definitely don’t want to spread them evenly from 0 to 1! If you do, you will have good precision in the brights, but very stark “intensity bands” in the dark colors. If everything was authored specifically for 3DFX, you would still have the fundamental problem with the dark bands, but more accurate blending and filtering. The problem was that artists made all of their textures in paint programs on conventional non-linear displays, so when they were drawn by 3DFX cards, they got the characteristic “washed out color” look. You can mathematically correct textures for differences in display gamma, but I didn’t really understand the issue back in the glQuake days, and we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have. Even today, tons of games don’t properly handle gamma across their textures and render targets. High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges.

items.body: BIS（美国商务部工业与安全局）出台远程算力访问新规，远程算力套利窗口正在关闭。先看新规要点：1）远程访问管制全球任何地区的数据中心中国公司及子公司提供超过1,200万TPP的算力（约相当于750张H100/H200量级，或约300张左右B200，具体视计算方式而定），相关先进计算芯片及服务器的出口、再出口和境内转移就需许可。许可逐案审批。 2）规则发布前已在提供大规模算力的数据中心，若要继续服务，须在生效后90天内取得许可，否则面临后续出口限制。 3）有限豁免：仅用于商业推荐系统（电商、社交媒体排名等，不生成文本/图像/音视频/软件）可豁免但须报备；生成式AI系统即使兼有推荐功能也不豁免。 4）新增五国许可：向印尼、马来西亚、新加坡、泰国、巴西出口/再出口/境内转移先进计算芯片均须许可（商务部长可增列其他国家）。美国总部公司可免许可但须月报。审查时会考虑目的国出口管制有效性及执法合作。 前两天《谁在“倒黄”》这篇长文聊到“境外云算力”越来越受限正在成为现实， 这两年中国头部公司（阿里、字节/抖音、腾讯等）大量通过马来西亚、新加坡、印尼、泰国等东南亚数据中心租用H100/H200/Blackwell算力进行训练。之前头部大模型公司把东南亚数据中心当作“准国内算力”使用，这次规则把这个主要workaround系统性地纳入许可。对需要十万卡级别训练的模型来说，这是成本、可用性和确定性的同步恶化。 远程先进算力通道被实质性收紧，会提高中国模型厂商训练的成本和难度，拖慢与美国前沿的追赶速度。 可以说美国正在试图封堵中国AI追赶过程中几乎所有重要的外部途径： 芯片管制更严格、 远程算力通道被压缩、前沿模型的反蒸馏措施越来越严格。 这算不算中国模型的“艰难时刻”？ 本条由@bitget_zh赞助，「Bitget 买美股：秒级入场，丝滑交易

items.title: 🔔 The Daily Semi-Cap — November 16, 2026 📊 SMH: $461.90 (-5.11% vs prior trading close) • Washington moved to close China’s remote-compute loophole, extending advanced-chip control
items.body: 🔔 The Daily Semi-Cap — November 16, 2026 📊 SMH: $461.90 (-5.11% vs prior trading close) • Washington moved to close China’s remote-compute loophole, extending advanced-chip controls to overseas data-center access. New licensing requirements also target shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. The risk now reaches cloud customers and cluster utilization—not just chips physically crossing into China. • Nvidia’s board is reportedly not considering reinstating Jensen Huang. Shares fell 4.12%. Tuesday’s report will test whether interim CEO Colette Kress can stabilize expectations while leadership uncertainty and tighter export controls complicate the company’s outlook. • Lambda deployed Nvidia co-packaged-optics switches connecting more than 10,000 Blackwell Ultra GPUs in Quebec. Its benchmarks showed unchanged throughput, 10.1% lower pod-level latency and optics running at 36°C versus 51°C. CPO is moving into commercial-scale clusters, shifting optical content toward engines and external lasers. • Powell Industries’ fiscal Q4 revenue rose 33% to $396.7M, with diluted EPS of $2.23. New orders reached $710M, including an approximately $85M data-center order; backlog hit $2.7B. A larger $250M LNG award underscores its broader industrial exposure. • Marvell and Penguin Solutions unveiled a memory-expansion collaboration combining recycled DDR4 through CXL with multi-rack photonic memory pooling. CXL cards are expected by year-end; photonic servers sample in H2 2027. The opportunity is better inference economics and memory utilization—not an immediate replacement for accelerator HBM. • Blackstone’s digital-infrastructure trust agreed to a $5B AWS property transaction covering 13 powered shells in Indiana and Mississippi. Blackstone takes 75%, AWS retains 25% and leases the properties back initially for 12 years. Hyperscalers are bringing outside real-estate capital into the buildout while retaining operating access. • Dell expanded its AI Factory lineup with direct-liquid-cooled Exascale storage designs and rack-scale management software supporting up to 100,000 devices. OpenManage Rack Scale and Fabric Manager are available now; data-platform upgrades start in December. • A new Harvard study estimated 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers consumed 68–99 TWh annually during May 2024–April 2025, with roughly 54% supplied by fossil fuels. That is historical, not today’s AI-only load, but highlights why generation mix and local grid constraints matter for campus siting.

items.title: Re: The new BIS rule I missed a provision yesterday. Under the new rule, chip designers in China and other restricted regions can no longer qualify for an exemption through the exi
items.body: Re: The new BIS rule I missed a provision yesterday. Under the new rule, chip designers in China and other restricted regions can no longer qualify for an exemption through the existing transistor-count verification process unless they have BIS status as an “approved” or “authorized” IC designer. Under the previous rule, a foundry or an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider could verify the transistor count to establish eligibility for an exemption. Now, BIS itself has to decide whether to grant one. As a result, foundries such as TSMC and Samsung Electronics, as well as OSAT providers such as ASE and Amkor, will need to conduct more thorough background checks on their customers.

items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.body: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. Show notes BFL explains what a still image, a moving camera and a soundtrack each contribute during training. FLUX 3 launch and research overview Watch and listen to the results of generating video and sound together. FLUX 3 Video demos See how the lab teaches a model to make a requested change while preserving the rest of an image. FLUX Kontext examples Andreas Blattmann co-created Stable Diffusion and co-invented the latent diffusion method behind it. Guest bio · Original research Dustin Podell led FLUX Kontext and was the lead author of SDXL. Dustin’s project credits · FLUX Kontext · SDXL The first Latent Space essay grew out of the Stable Diffusion release. external_articles.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
external_articles.body:
Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades.

Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round.

Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago.

For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it.

Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow.

Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors.

Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before.

Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA?

A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain.

A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before.

If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner.

Q: What’s an example of that in practice ?

A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity.

In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication.

Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today.

Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms?

A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned.

As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing.

For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum .

Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly.

Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else?

A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing.

If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.”

That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them.

Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen?

A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable.

And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful.

Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain?

A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip.

Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week.

We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it.

Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting.

Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward?

A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200 . The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan.

The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. That kept production moving, but would not solve the throughput requirement of full production.

As with any operations problem, the root cause had many elements to it: test tray assembly, test tray design, automation hardware design, automation control software, product yield. From all viewpoints, it was a difficult problem to resolve quickly.

That’s when we executed the NVIDIA swarm. Teams from NVIDIA design engineering, operations industrial, and product and test engineering, as well as from Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate the line before the scale ramp hit.

This is not an unusual occurrence when there is a problem in operations. All teams at NVIDIA are street fighters — action-oriented, and know no organizational boundaries. We say that “the mission is the boss,” but we also live “the mission is the boss.”

Q: What makes this work so exciting for you?

A: Operations is a very empowering place to be at NVIDIA. Our team is designing and implementing changes to the supply chain constantly to meet the strong demand of our new products. The challenges are understandably high, but we’re always given the resources we need to be successful. The only thing between our goals and our success is our own creativity. That is exhilarating.

items.title: $NVDA NVIDIA: THE COMPLETE READ-THROUGH THE THREE CHARTS TOGETHER Spot is making new lows on heavy but decelerating volume while 18-month call and put vol are both making near year
items.body: $NVDA NVIDIA: THE COMPLETE READ-THROUGH THE THREE CHARTS TOGETHER Spot is making new lows on heavy but decelerating volume while 18-month call and put vol are both making near year highs. Those facts together describe a market that is de-risking the cash position and simultaneously paying up for long-dated optionality in both directions. The stock is being sold by holders reducing exposure; the vol is being bought by people who need convexity because the outcome distribution has genuinely widened. Neither side is capitulating and neither side is confident. That is a binary market, priced as one, 24 hours before the event that resolves it. WHAT THE SELLOFF IS Four drivers, in order of weight. First, positioning: prime brokerage had AI hardware at roughly 40% of hedge fund portfolios this summer, the trimming started before the resignation, and a crowded trade unwinds on its own schedule regardless of news. Second, a coordination point: the SemiAnalysis revision, dated Friday, leaked into public circulation this morning and gave every holder the same anchor on the same day, in a thin premarket, the day before the print. Third, a funding drain: the buildout's marginal funding mechanism has rotated from free cash flow to debt to equity, and Anthropic prices Wednesday at a size that forces room to be made across the complex. Fourth, the case itself: Nvidia carries a governance and regulatory overhang none of its peers have, which is why it sits near the bottom of the damage table despite not being the most commodity-exposed name. WHAT THE SELLOFF IS NOT It is not a confirmed fundamental turn. Checked against the primary data: capex consensus is still revised sharply up versus January with no hyperscaler guide down; conference takeaways through last week are raises and reaffirmations, Celestica guiding 2027 up 90%, Foxconn booked out 1.5 years; Taiwan October sales printed +63.8% year on year with no downward revisions today; GPU rentals are flat like for like with the marketplace actually up. The only genuine soft spot in the data is spot NAND pricing. Daniel Newman made the matching point from outside: SemiAnalysis's three stated drivers cannot arithmetically produce 40% ASP cuts, so either the note is assumption putty, or its unstated driver is the China-linked demand the enforcement lane is now removing. Either way, no primary source has cut anything. THE VOL READ The 35-delta 18-month call went from the year's low of 37.33 on October 12 to 44.44 today. The matching put went from 37.96 on October 6, the day spot made its high, to 45.84 today. The two wings have risen in near parallel, the call by 7.12 points and the put by 7.88 points, at a tenor far too long to be print-week noise. The put now trades 1.40 points above the call, versus only 0.08 point a year ago. Read it as the market's probability statement: this is a repricing of variance, not a directional options bid. Both tails are being paid for at the same time. Part of that is mechanical, dealers widening a distribution that now includes a CEO search, a Treasury secretary demanding bank-grade compliance, and an interim CEO's first print. The structure is also consistent with flows on both sides: replacement buying would lift the call wing when holders sell stock and rent the upside back, while protection buying would lift the put wing for holders who are not selling. Part of it is specific to the right tail: after the President said today he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated, the reinstatement scenario is a live right tail that did not exist a week ago and has to be priced by anyone short vol. Elevated long-dated vol is also why defined-risk structures own this tape and outright stock ownership just suffers it. THE CASE OVERLAY Nvidia-specific, unchanged by today's tape. The BIS remote-access rule issued this morning is the first government act in the case's lane but it is prospective rulemaking, names no company, and leaves Megaspeed off the Entity List, so no named government action against the company or Megaspeed has occurred. Trump's reinstatement remarks are a stance, not a board act, and they cut against Bessent's outside-CEO push with the board's answer due around November 25. The falsifiers stand: no search pause, no board silence past the print, no softening 8-K. Nothing today touches the conclusion that Huang does not return. THE PRINT IS THE CLEARING EVENT Three reads tomorrow night decide the next quarter. The Q4 guide against consensus of $124.73B: at or above roughly $124B is in line, $120B to $124B is soft, below $120B is a hard guide down. The FY28 growth language: the FQ2 call's approximately 70% is now the most contested sentence in the stock, because the SemiAnalysis path has the accelerator market growing about 21% in 2028 with Nvidia's share falling; reaffirming 70% breaks the SemiAnalysis anchor publicly, qualifying or dropping it installs that path as consensus and makes Morgan Stanley's cut, FY28 EPS $15.01 to $13.37, look like the first domino. And Kress's register, operator or caretaker, which prices the succession vacuum the Stratechery obituary described today: a company organized as one man's exoskeleton, whose supply chain ran on his handshake. SCENARIOS If the guide holds and the language survives: the SemiAnalysis anchor breaks, long-dated vol crushes hard, the crowded unwind is already eight sessions and roughly 3 billion shares old, and Anthropic prices into a cleared tape on Wednesday. If the guide breaks below $120B or the FY28 language is dropped: the SemiAnalysis path becomes the sell-side template, the November 12 intraday low of 148.80 is 4.5% away and likely goes, and the exit question reopens. The middle outcome, a soft guide with the language intact, keeps the grind alive into the December hearings and the November 25 board deadline. READ-ACROSS Refiners are insulated and green today: cash-generative, no AI capex exposure, untouched while the AI infrastructure names take the damage. Semicap equipment is where the timing risk sits: the bid is expected to return after the Anthropic listing and this print clear, really in January, and equipment names parked near their lows may not see it if the bid comes late. Memory is the most commodity-exposed segment if the rotation thesis is right, and the labs are confirming the rotation daily, ahead of the hardware by about 3 points again this afternoon. The neoclouds carry the worst of both worlds in the SemiAnalysis path and in the reported pullback in Nvidia guarantees: most cut exposure, least funding resilience, and a patron whose willingness to backstop them was personal to the man who just left. BOTTOM LINE The selloff is real as a positioning event and unconfirmed as a fundamental one. The three charts are the market pricing the widest outcome distribution in a year into a binary 24 hours. The only two things that change the read before tomorrow night are a break of the November 12 intraday low at 148.80, which has not happened, and new primary evidence of an actual capex cut, which does not exist in the data.

items.title: Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary. Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue ge
items.body: Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary. Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue gets revised down later. I do think it's important to model in capex forecasts dropping past 2028, due to the current reflexive nature of AI selloffs, rate hikes, etc. The drawn out duration of Iran War doesn't help, Jensen leaving $NVDA certainty draws concerns over Nvidia's ecosystem. But any catalyst, like if Iran War ends, can also change sentiment in a heartbeat (since bearish positioning is overwhelming). - It's also clear financing has been tightening, since OpenAI only managed to raise $11B of their original $30B target so far. - Markets are reacting enthusiastically to companies like $TE doing a $100M ATM today (nuking valuations) - Although the "guppy" sector is probably the most sensitive to financing + rate changes. On bright side... Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN seem to be adjusting by getting 100% capex prepayments or 90% GPU prepayments from their counterparties. What I'd argue though is lower aggregate capex does not apply uniformly in supply chains. - Mid-high range lasers for NPO/CPO are still sold out, as seen with $LITE now starting negotiations for 2030 capacity. - MLCCs are seeing further tightening as content usage goes up for AI servers - ABF substrates to InP substrates not really going anywhere. If content per system goes up 10X-15X, capacity expands at 2-3X Y/Y, and capex drops 28%. And content is so cheap that you can triple order and screw over competitors with wafer supply... I'm pretty confident you'll see acceleration upstream in bottlenecks from optical components to substrates despite potential aggregate capex dropping. Another rant is: -I keep seeing this argument that "low P/E is a warning for cyclical that's going to crash" but these are just clown takes Nobody seems to analyze duration scenarios like capacity expansion vs. content changes vs. demand. to actually see how long those earnings last. If everyone seems to be exiting DDR2 lines, there's probably going be more tightness in 2027 despite consume demand weakening, even if it looks like it's low P/E. - Also for concerns about CPO "delays", the same components like lasers are used for NPO. You'll still see 150-200mW NPO lasers or ELS NPO using the same 300–400+ mW lasers as CPO. We'll just see acceleration with NPO as a bridge if CPO gets delayed and higher range lasers likely to remain in a severe shortage. - Feels like markets have also completely discredited the merit of take/pay price floor LTAs as well that companies like SK Hynix to Samsung have. If contractual agreements hold up, memory players look very undervalued. TLDR: - I think it's important to model in capex decreasing to numbers like -30% in hypothetical downside sceanrios. Given AI profitability, it's clearly not sustainable for hyperscalers to aggregately increase capex $500B or $1T+ Y/Y, and that's never been a case I've argued. - This is also not the same thing as demand destruction that markets are overreacting to now (which haven't happened yet). - We can see demand revisions for GPUs, ASICs, and heavier cost parts of the supply chain, while acceleration increases elsewhere. The nuances market miss by indiscriminately selling everything is going to present compelling opportunities when the dust settles. I think in the end institutions are probably going to end up owning more of the same names retail discovered early on. Anyway, I think it's a good idea to try and survive until more earnings comes out.

items.body: - Lambda announced a large-scale NVIDIA CPO deployment connecting 10,000+ Blackwell Ultra GPUs in Quebec. - Each Quantum-X Photonics switch features 144 × 800G ports, liquid cooling, and 18 field-replaceable ELS modules. - Lambda reported identical throughput, with latency reduced 3.8% at rack scale and 10.1% at pod scale. - Median optics temperature dropped from 51°C to 36°C, with improved signal integrity. - $NVDA claims up to 5x better power efficiency, 15x higher reliability, and 75% fewer lasers. > CPO has moved beyond demonstrations into a commercial-scale AI cluster, with operator-reported benchmark data. > The 15x reliability figure remains a vendor claim, not an independently verified long-term field failure rate. > CPO could shift optical value from pluggable modules toward optical engines, ELS, advanced packaging, and wafer-level testing. > $COHR and $LITE have relevant laser and optical component exposure, but direct supply to Lambda's deployment remains unconfirmed. > $FORM, $KEYS, and $TER could benefit indirectly from increasing optical-engine production test complexity, subject to customer adoption and equipment orders. > NVIDIA's collaboration with TSMC on COUPE is established, but Lambda-specific optical engine yields and packaging volumes remain undisclosed. > Switch shipments, optical engine yield, ELS volumes, and field failure rates matter more for measuring CPO commercialization than the 10,000-GPU headline alone. > Using 4x fewer lasers means CPO adoption does not translate directly into proportional laser revenue growth. > $COHR and $LITE fell sharply intraday on November 16 amid broader AI hardware selling, even as real-world CPO adoption advanced. > NVIDIA's November 17 earnings call could provide important updates on CPO demand, shipments, and manufacturing capacity.

external_articles.title: AGENTS.md for making Blender videos with an AI coding agent, plus the mechanical watch brief
external_articles.body:
Instructions for an AI coding agent (Claude Code, omp, Kimi Code and similar) that makes Blender videos for you. Save this file as AGENTS.md in an empty folder, open your coding agent in that folder, and tell it what video you want. Each video gets its own subfolder.

Credit: based on the prompt by @MrTacticalX from the X article "How to make Claude build 3D videos in Blender" .

Hi Claude. I want you to make 3D videos for me in Blender. I can't code, so you do all the technical work and keep your explanations simple. Follow these instructions.

Only run Blender in background mode (blender -b) with your own Python scripts, at low priority so my PC stays usable. Never open the Blender window on my screen. Build the whole scene in code: models, materials, lights, camera, animation and physics. You can also use free CC0 textures and models from Poly Haven, e.g. bark, wood or a sky, unless I say not to. Never in comparisons (see Step 8).

Ask me what I want in the video. If I don't know, suggest three ideas, each one object with satisfying motion or physics, e.g. a tree shaken until its leaves fall, a Rubik's cube that solves itself then shatters, or a pumpkin that carves itself.

Before you build anything, turn my idea into a short plan with these six parts and show it to me:

Wait for me to say yes before you build.

This is the most important rule. Don't go straight to the final render. Work in rounds:

Render with Cycles with the denoiser on, then turn the frames into an MP4 with ffmpeg (H.264, yuv420p, AAC sound) so it plays on phones and X. Then make me a contact sheet: one image with 12 frames from across the video, so I can check the whole thing at a glance.

If I ask another AI model for the same video so I can compare you side by side, protect the comparison:

I'll just tell you what's wrong, e.g. "the camera is too far" or "the leaves look like paper". Have the sub agent fix exactly that, keep everything I liked, and render again. Add the time and cost of the fix to the total. Not in comparisons. There, both entries stay exactly as the models made them.

Only count the agents that built the video (all of them if it's a team), not your own planning and checking. Note the time when the build starts. When it's done, add up their tokens from their log files (Claude Code saves each sub agent's log as a .jsonl file under ~/.claude/projects, and every reply in it lists its tokens). In a comparison, do the same for the other model from its own log (ask me where it is if you can't find it). Then tell me:

Put the final video in a folder called "Finished videos" on my Desktop (make it if it doesn't exist), then open the video on my PC so I can watch it straight away.

Then ask if I want to post it. If I do, write me a short post to go with the video, with the time and cost on their own lines, e.g. "⏱2 hr 42 min" and "💰$41.52". 🚀

One last thing: a detailed video can take hours, so remind me to keep the PC on and Claude Code open until it's done.
