items.title: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE WHY NVIDIA HAS NO SIDE B OR SIDE C: THE UNDERWRITING QUESTION The obvious question after the Financial Times reported that Nvidia carries up to $900 million o
items.body: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE WHY NVIDIA HAS NO SIDE B OR SIDE C: THE UNDERWRITING QUESTION The obvious question after the Financial Times reported that Nvidia carries up to $900 million of Side A only D&O insurance, with no Side B and no Side C, is why a company of this size would leave its own balance sheet uninsured. The answer being whispered is that the company could not have survived the diligence: that applying for entity coverage would have exposed what was going on inside. That theory gets the mechanism wrong, and the correct mechanism is more interesting. D&O underwriters do not investigate anybody. What applying for Side B and Side C actually requires is a signature: a set of representations, made after polling the board and the executive team, about what the company and its officers know. Here is what that process involves, what differs between the three sides of the policy, and what follows for Nvidia. WHAT UNDERWRITERS ACTUALLY DO An underwriter pricing a large public company's D&O program works from paper and public data. The broker assembles a submission: the application, the last twelve months of SEC filings, and the indemnification provisions of the charter and bylaws. The carrier reviews financials, claims history, market capitalization, share volatility, credit spreads, ownership concentration, and litigation history, benchmarks the company against peers, and models securities claim frequency and severity. On large placements there is a management presentation, typically the CFO or treasurer with accounting and legal staff, the CEO occasionally, where underwriters ask questions directly. What no source describes, in any carrier form, broker guide, or academic study of the process, is an underwriter auditing internal records, interviewing employees, or hunting for undisclosed misconduct. An underwriter cannot diligence what exists only inside the building. That limitation is exactly why the law puts the weight somewhere else: on what the company signs. THE PAPER EVERY BUYER SIGNS A carrier application for a public company program asks, among other things: whether there have been, in the last five years, any pending civil, criminal, administrative, or arbitration proceedings against the company or any person proposed for insurance; whether any claim, or notice of circumstances that could give rise to a claim, has been reported to a prior insurer; any regulatory cease and desist orders or written agreements with an agency; the company's insider trading policy; senior management changes; and contemplated mergers, acquisitions, or securities offerings. Then comes the question the whole structure turns on. One carrier form asks it this way: is the undersigned, or any director or officer proposed for this insurance, aware of any fact, circumstance, or situation which he or she has reason to believe might result in any future claim under the policy? The form then states the consequence in capitals: if knowledge of any such fact exists, any claim subsequently arising from it shall be excluded from coverage. This is not a signature an officer gives casually. The standard practitioner guidance is that the company should poll its senior executives and board members before signing, in a process that communicates the importance of the inquiry, and keep the polling record, because the record is later used to show the company took reasonable steps to answer honestly. Carrier signature blocks say the same thing in contract language: the signer represents, after reasonable inquiry, that the answers are true, and undertakes to update them if anything changes before the policy incepts. Crucially, buying Side A does not skip any of this. A standalone primary Side A application from a major carrier asks, about the individuals, whether they have been involved in written demands, civil or criminal proceedings, formal or informal investigations, or service of a subpoena under an SEC formal investigative order, across securities laws, shareholder and derivative suits, and employment matters. It then asks the same prior knowledge question, and its consequence is drafted person by person: no coverage for a claim against a person who knew. The questions are the same. What changes between the sides is everything downstream of the answers. SIDE A VERSUS SIDE B VERSUS SIDE C: THE DILIGENCE LADDER Side A, primary: the person tier. The inquiry centers on the individuals: their involvement in suits, demands, and investigations, and what they know. The underwriter's analytical work is the company's solvency and its indemnification gap, read in a direction that surprises people: a weaker balance sheet raises Side A risk, because Side A pays precisely when the company cannot or will not indemnify. Failure consequences are contained by design. Severability means one officer's knowledge is not imputed to another, and the exclusion bites only on the person who knew. Side B: the documentary tier. Side B reimburses the company for the defense costs and settlements it advances or pays for its officers, so its pricing document is the charter and bylaw indemnification machinery itself: whether advancement is mandatory or permissive, how broad the indemnity runs, what repayment undertakings exist. The underwriter prices legal obligations and the company's liquidity to advance. Proceedings history matters here as a predictor of how much cash the company will lay out. Side C: the modeling tier, and the deepest diligence in the program. Side C covers the company itself, which for a public company means securities claims. This is where the quantitative work lives: a year of filings read for disclosure quality, guidance practices, restatements, and control problems, and entity claim modeling off market cap, volatility, credit spreads, regulatory investigations, deal activity, and concentrated holders. The management presentation belongs to this tier: underwriters meet the people whose disclosures they are insuring. Side C also carries the largest premiums and the securities retention, the deductible like amount the company pays itself, which is where diligence conclusions become the company's own money at risk. Excess Side A DIC: the lightest tier in the market. Dedicated Side A Difference in Conditions policies sit on top of a program and protect individuals if the tower beneath them fails. Their carriers do almost no diligence of their own. They take the primary policy and its application, ride on the primary underwriting, and substitute contract design for scrutiny: broader terms, typically a single conduct exclusion, no retention, and drop down coverage when an underlying insurer cannot pay or tries to rescind. The marketing language from major carriers is explicit: absolutely non-rescindable, full severability of the application. THE IMPUTATION TRAP Modern D&O policies sever the application between insured persons, so an innocent director is not destroyed by a colleague's misstatement. But where a policy includes entity coverage, the bargain has a second half. In current carrier forms, the knowledge of a small designated set is imputed to the company. One major carrier's specimen states it in a single sentence: only the knowledge of the CEO or CFO will be imputed to the Organization. Practitioner guidance advises keeping that set as narrow as possible, preferably no more than the CEO, CFO, and general counsel, precisely because it can void the company's coverage. Follow what that means at the entity tier. The validity of the company's Side B and Side C coverage rests on the knowledge of the two offices at the center of any crisis: the chief executive and the chief financial officer. At the Side A tier, no such exposure exists. There is no entity insured, there is nothing to impute knowledge to, and a bad answer costs only the person who gave it. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE PAPER IS WRONG The remedies run on a ladder, and the cases show each rung. First, exclusion. The claim arising from the undisclosed circumstance is excluded by the application's own agreed language. No intent needs proving. In a 2022 Delaware case, Infinity Q, a firm bought three new excess layers and signed warranty letters for each stating that nobody proposed for insurance knew of facts that might give rise to a claim. Months earlier it had received SEC letters opening an inquiry into its fund valuations, and internal texts showed the signers discussing that inquiry and the need to buy more insurance. Nothing was disclosed. When the inquiry became an enforcement action, a class action, and a criminal investigation, the court held the warranty letters' prior knowledge exclusion precluded coverage under those excess layers. The primary policy, placed without such a warranty, paid. Second, person scoped denial. Where the form severs properly, coverage dies only for the insureds who knew. After HealthSouth's fraud surfaced and its carriers sought rescission over an application that incorporated fraudulent financials, the court confined rescission to insured persons who personally made a knowing misrepresentation. Third, rescission of the entity coverage, where the misrepresented knowledge belongs to the imputation set: the signer, the CEO, the CFO. Fourth, full rescission, rare under modern forms but not theoretical. In Cutter and Buck, the CFO who signed the application knew the materials submitted in the underwriting process were materially false, including statements made at an underwriting meeting and on calls with the carrier. The court held the insurer could rescind the entire program, and that the policy's severability clause, as written, imputed the signing officer's knowledge to every other director and officer. Note the detail: what is said in the underwriting presentation is part of the representation record, not small talk. THE RENEWAL WRINKLE One more piece of machinery decides whether any of this was live in a given year. On a plain renewal of existing coverage with an incumbent carrier, standard practitioner doctrine holds that the warranty question is emphatically not re-asked, because the policyholder is entitled to continuity of coverage across successive years. The representation moments with teeth are new placements, carrier changes, restructures, and purchases of new or increased limits, the last of which requires a fresh warranty statement for the new layer on any side of the policy. A company that simply rolls an existing tower forward may sign nothing new. A company that changes the shape of its tower signs fresh paper for the changed parts. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR NVIDIA Start with what the A only structure does not do. It does not avoid the questions. If the reported $900 million is a primary standalone Side A program, Nvidia's placement answered the investigations question, including informal investigations and SEC subpoenas, and the prior knowledge question, on a signature given after reasonable inquiry, the same discipline any ABC buyer faces. If part of the tower is excess DIC, the top layers were placed on the lightest diligence that exists in this market. What the structure does avoid is two specific things. It avoids the entity premium, at a market capitalization where entity coverage is the most expensive paper in the tower, for a company holding roughly $99 billion of cash and marketable securities that can plainly self insure. And it avoids the imputation tier: there is no Side B to reimburse and no Side C to void, so no coverage the company owns depends on what its CEO and CFO knew when the paper was signed. If a representation anywhere in the tower was wrong, the loss is contained to individuals who knew, inside a severed, largely non rescindable structure. The same wrong answer inside an ABC program could have taken the company's own coverage with it. Two explanations fit those facts. The mundane one: a deliberate, sophisticated self insurance decision, entity risk retained because it is affordable, individu

items.title: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE What a total disaster. Unbelievable. Astronomical miss. ----------------------- NVIDIA, INSURANCE, AND THE CREDIT MARKET: THE FULL PICTURE Nvidia's executives
items.body: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE What a total disaster. Unbelievable. Astronomical miss. ----------------------- NVIDIA, INSURANCE, AND THE CREDIT MARKET: THE FULL PICTURE Nvidia's executives insured themselves. Its investors were left holding the risk. Per the Financial Times, the company bought $900 million of insurance protecting its directors and officers personally, and bought none of the coverage that protects the company itself: no Side B to reimburse the defense costs Nvidia is legally required to advance to those same executives while their cases run, and no Side C to cover the securities class action that has now been filed against the company. Every dollar of that exposure comes straight out of the balance sheet the shareholders own. The executives' legal bills are advanced from investor funds. Any settlement is paid from investor funds. The people whose conduct created the liability are protected to $900 million, and the owners who did nothing wrong are the insurer of last resort. This is not how public companies arrange this. More than 80 percent of them buy all three sides of the policy, and the practitioners who sell this coverage call an A only structure very seldom seen. If the allocation was deliberate, the board decided whose risk mattered, and it was not the shareholders'. If it was not deliberate, it is worse: a company worth $4 trillion walked into the most foreseeable litigation in its history with its own side of the policy missing, and nobody in the building noticed. Either way, the people at risk are not the people who caused it. The viral version of this story, that Nvidia bought no insurance at all and will be buried under litigation, is wrong, and the claim that its credit spreads blew out to records is stale. The truth is sharper than both. The exposure is real, it is bounded, the individuals are protected to an unusually high standard, the owners carry the company's share, and the credit market priced all of it months ago and has started to retrace. WHAT NVIDIA ACTUALLY BOUGHT Per the Financial Times, sourced to two people familiar with the policy, Nvidia placed through broker Aon a Side A D&O policy with a limit of up to $900 million, with Beazley, AIG and Chubb among the insurers. It did not buy Side B or Side C coverage. No insurer or the company has confirmed this. Nvidia's SEC filings disclose nothing about its insurance structure, which is normal; D&O program structure is not an SEC disclosure item. One filed document matters: Nvidia's form of indemnity agreement, on file since 2006, contractually requires the company to obtain and maintain D&O insurance naming its officers and directors as insureds. A total failure to buy D&O cover would breach Nvidia's own contracts. HOW D&O INSURANCE WORKS A standard D&O policy has three sides. Side A covers directors and officers personally when the company cannot or will not indemnify them, most importantly in shareholder derivative suits, where Delaware law bars the company from indemnifying settlements. Side B reimburses the company when it indemnifies its directors and officers, which companies are generally required to do, including advancing their legal costs as cases proceed. Side C covers the company itself when it is sued, and for a public company that means securities class actions. Nvidia, per the FT, bought only Side A. The individuals are protected to $900 million. The company's own costs are not insured. WHAT THE COMPANY FACES, UNINSURED A securities class action filed November 9 in federal court in California accuses the company and Huang of false and misleading statements about the founder's relationship with Alice Huang, with a class period of October 9, 2025 to November 8, 2026. One widely circulated summary describes this suit as a case about channel inventory and cryptocurrency mining demand. That is the 2018 era litigation, a different case. The current complaint is about the relationship and what was said about it. Without Side C, Nvidia pays its own defense costs and any settlement or judgment in the current case from its balance sheet. Without Side B, Nvidia also pays from its own funds the defense costs it must advance to its current and former officers in every proceeding, including Huang's. If an officer is ultimately adjudicated to have committed fraud, advanced costs are repayable, but the company carries them in the meantime. A derivative suit is the most likely next filing. Shareholders sue the directors on the company's behalf for oversight and loyalty failures: what the board knew about the relationship, about the assurances given to the company's own general counsel and chief marketing officer, and about diversion red flags, and when it knew it. In a derivative settlement, the company typically pays the plaintiffs' legal fees, and any governance reforms become its cost as well. WHAT THE INSURANCE MARKET'S OWN ANALYSTS MODEL Bloomberg Intelligence's insurance team, writing on November 12 before the FT story appeared, modeled Nvidia's insured D&O loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars, and named Chubb, AIG, Berkshire Hathaway and Travelers as the likely leading carriers in the US D&O market for an exposure of this kind. Two points follow. First, an insured loss in the hundreds of millions is consistent with the FT's structure rather than contradicted by it: under a Side A only program, the insured losses are the individual side losses, derivative settlements and defense costs, and that is exactly the layer BI is sizing. Second, BI's follow up work on November 13 cautioned that some settlements may not be fully covered by insurance and that shareholder litigation of this kind could take until 2029 or 2030 to reach material resolution. That timeline is the honest one. This is a multi year litigation stack, not a near term cash event. THE SIZE OF THE EXPOSURE Numbers, since the burial narrative never provides any. On the insured side, Bloomberg Intelligence models the D&O loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars. That is the layer the $900 million Side A tower stands behind, and it is the layer most likely to be paid by insurers. On the company's uninsured side, the arithmetic is just as bounded. A securities settlement in a governance case of this kind, defense costs across the class and derivative actions, and the advancement obligations together realistically run in the low hundreds of millions, with a severe outcome reaching toward $1 billion. For calibration, the largest securities class action settlements in history top out in the low single digit billions, and those were fabricated financials cases. This is a concealment and governance case, a category that settles for far less. Stack every adverse outcome on top of each other. A securities settlement at the severe end, plus an export control settlement at the scale of the largest precedents on record, Seagate at $300 million and Applied Materials at $252.5 million, plus a federal corporate resolution and years of fees, and the all in worst case lands in the area of $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion. Against that: $99 billion of cash and marketable securities, and a quarter that will print roughly $108 billion of revenue. The worst realistic case is about 2 percent of the liquidity on hand. Painful, embarrassing, and financially irrelevant are three different things. This exposure is the first two. WHAT NO INSURANCE WOULD HAVE PAID ANYWAY Export control penalties are not covered. A Bureau of Industry and Security settlement, a Justice Department corporate resolution, and SEC penalties are corporate regulatory outcomes. D&O insurance does not pay them, whether a company buys Side A only or a full tower. The board's internal investigation, run by outside counsel since November 10, is the company's own cost under any structure. Fines against individuals are uninsurable as a matter of public policy. If Huang faces personal criminal exposure, no policy pays it. Insurance covers defense costs, not culpability. So the insurance gap is confined to one layer: private civil litigation. The class action, derivative claims, and advancement obligations. That layer is real, and it is also the smallest of the stacks facing this company. WHAT THE INDIVIDUALS FACE, AND WHAT COVERS THEM For the directors and officers, the structure is close to optimal, and possibly deliberately so. In a traditional combined policy, the three sides share one limit. A large settlement paid for the company erodes the same tower that protects the individuals. Lawyers call this the shared limit problem, and it has bitten directors in past cases when the entity's claims consumed the coverage. A dedicated Side A tower cannot be touched by the company's settlements. Nvidia's reported $900 million sits behind the individuals only, and Side A is exactly the side that responds where the law forbids indemnification: derivative settlements, and any situation where the company itself is insolvent or refuses to pay. The directors facing an oversight claim are covered to a limit that is, by the standards of companies that buy Side A only, very large. A Willis survey of Fortune 1000 companies found Side A only buyers typically carry $50 million to $200 million. Huang personally is covered for defense costs, subject to the standard conduct exclusion, which only bites on a final adjudication of deliberate fraud. His forfeited unvested equity, reported at $108 million, is an exit economics question, not an insurance one: no policy restores it. WHAT THE CREDIT MARKET IS ACTUALLY SAYING The second circulating claim is that Nvidia's 5 year CDS has blown out to 144.5 basis points, near a record, as the board weighed the CEO's fate. Read the terminal instead. Nvidia 5 year CDS closed Friday, November 13 at 128.6 basis points, and it tightened 10.2 basis points that day. The year's high was 143.9 basis points, printed on October 30, roughly two weeks before the board accepted Huang's resignation. The year's low was 38.7 basis points on February 2, and the average across the year is 59 basis points. The widening did not start with the resignation. Spreads sat near 40 basis points through the spring, climbed through the summer to the 60 to 85 range, and accelerated in October. In other words, protection buyers were pricing this story months before it became public, the peak came before the climax, and at the moment of maximum headline stress the spread is retracing. The momentum indicator on the chart, MACD, has crossed down: the widening move is exhausting itself. Context matters on the level as well. 128 basis points is a headline and event premium, not a solvency signal. Nvidia held about $99 billion in cash and marketable securities at its last balance sheet date, against minimal debt. The CDS market is pricing governance uncertainty and hedging demand around a binary news cycle. It is not pricing default, and it is not pricing a litigation burden the balance sheet cannot carry. A company whose entire stacked worst case across every proceeding amounts to about 2 percent of its liquidity does not get buried. It gets a line item. THE GENUINE OPEN QUESTIONS Three are worth naming. First, the sourcing. The insurance story rests on two anonymous sources in one newspaper, building on a trade publication's report of the limit. It may be exactly right. It is not confirmed, and the filings cannot confirm it. Second, rescission. Insurers can seek to rescind a policy if the application for it misrepresented known circumstances. D&O applications ask what the applicants know. Who signed Nvidia's application, when, and what they knew about the matters now in litigation is the kind of question that decides whether a tower actually pays, years from now, in a coverage lawsuit nobody has filed yet. Third, investigations. Whether the policy responds to the costs of government investigations of individuals varies by policy wording. With congressional subpoenas in play and a federal inquiry open,

items.title: TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/14/26 Overnight, Reuters reported that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's own general counsel and chief marketing officer in w
items.body: TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/14/26 Overnight, Reuters reported that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's own general counsel and chief marketing officer in writing that his interactions with Alice Huang and Megaspeed were standard business dealings, the House chairs' 8 p.m. deadline for his written acceptance of the December 1 interview passed with nothing public, and a filings-based reconstruction put $5,353 million of Nvidia's formerly Singapore-billed revenue with China and Hong Kong headquartered buyers. Super Micro denied on the record that Megaspeed was ever its customer, a sitting administration official argued Huang should have been warned the way a congressman once was, and the street kept repricing the overhang: HSBC cut its target by more than half, and a billionaire holder said he will make no further investment in Nvidia without Huang. THE ASSURANCES INSIDE NVIDIA • Reuters reported today that Huang misled several of Nvidia's leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang: in two separate messages in October 2026, and in other messages, Huang told Nvidia leaders including Teter and Wagonfeld that his interactions with Alice Huang and Megaspeed reflected "standard business dealings with customers" and affirmed the routine nature of his interactions with Megaspeed, according to two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence reviewed by Reuters. Reuters reviewed several October exchanges, on condition of not quoting them verbatim, and is the first to report this correspondence. • The people said Huang gave similar assurances in the autumn of 2025, in response to press queries; Reuters did not review the 2025 exchanges. Huang also discussed taking legal action against The New York Times over its October 2025 article drawing attention to his public meetings with Alice Huang; neither Huang nor Nvidia filed a lawsuit and the Times received no legal demand. • Reuters verified photos showing the pair together in the US, China and elsewhere dating back to December 2023; when the relationship became intimate remains unclear. Teter did not respond to comment requests, Wagonfeld did not immediately respond, and Huang's representative and Nvidia declined to comment. This is Reuters' own reporting: the misled parties here are Nvidia's own senior executives, not investigators, and Reuters offers no evidence about what Huang knew of the intelligence or export-control concerns. THE DEADLINE PASSES IN SILENCE • The 8 p.m. ET November 13 deadline in the three chairs' November 12 letter, for Huang to confirm in writing that he would sit for the December 1 closed-door transcribed interview, passed with no public confirmation, refusal, subpoena issuance, or committee statement in the case record's coverage through about 10:16 p.m. ET. The only post addressing the deadline's outcome in the window noted that the deadline came and went and that no confirmation from Huang had been made public. That is the public record only: whether a written confirmation was delivered through non-public channels is unverified, and nothing public appeared on Tim Teter's December 2 confirmation either. The chairs' stated next step, a House Foreign Affairs Committee subpoena to compel, is now in play. • Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a House Intelligence Committee member, said on CNBC on November 13, in words verified against the full transcript of the clip: "We want more facts. We want to understand exactly the timeline here and the information at hand." He said the official response from Huang had not come in yet, that three committees with jurisdiction had asked Huang to testify and "threatened yesterday to issue subpoenas to get the information we need," and that the key question is whether advanced chips were diverted to China. Citing Intelligence Committee ranking member Jim Himes, he said "it's still unclear if she was a spy or just unwitting in all this." THE SINGAPORE NUMBERS, RECAST • A filings-based reconstruction published by Schulz Research today quantifies where Nvidia's Singapore-billed revenue went when the company switched its geographic footnote from customer billing location to direct-customer headquarters location. Matching Note 13 of the original Q2 FY26 Form 10-Q against the recast comparative columns in Note 13 of the Q2 FY27 Form 10-Q, on the same $90,805 million first-half revenue base: $19,173 million of first-half FY26 Singapore invoices disappeared from the Singapore line alongside a $1,416 million reduction in Other, a total reclassification of $20,589 million. • Of that total, $14,373 million (69.8 percent) moved into the United States, $5,353 million (26.0 percent) moved into China including Hong Kong, and $863 million (4.2 percent) moved into Taiwan. In Q2 alone the United States share lifted from 50.2 percent to 70.4 percent, and China including Hong Kong rose 43.9 percent, from $2,769 million to $3,985 million. The reconstruction is a single practitioner account's arithmetic on two filed 10-Qs, read in full in the case record; the desk did not independently recompute the matching, and the $5,353 million is reclassified revenue by headquarters location, not a diversion figure. The same post asserts, as its own reporting and not verified elsewhere in the window, that Dell confirmed halting sales to Singapore partner Aperia International in February 2025. SUPER MICRO DENIES THE CHANNEL • Super Micro Computer, through a spokesperson statement carried identically across the tape on November 13, stated: "Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer." The company said it has been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, and that it voluntarily provided information and is engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date. The statement is the company's on-record denial of any customer relationship with Megaspeed, and it narrows the prong opened by Bloomberg's November 12 reporting that the U.S. is probing whether Alice Huang helped smuggle Super Micro products: whatever the probe examines, Super Micro's position is that no direct customer channel to Megaspeed existed. THE ADMINISTRATION PUSHES BACK • David Sacks, the White House AI and crypto czar, said on the All-In podcast, in words verified against the full transcript of the clip, that Huang's treatment contrasts with the handling of Rep. Eric Swalwell's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Fang Fang: Swalwell, then on the House Intelligence Committee, was given a defensive briefing, said he cut off the relationship, and kept both his seat in Congress and his seat on the Intelligence Committee, with no resignation thought necessary. • Sacks argued that if the national security state was worried Huang possessed national security secrets he might leak to someone suspected of being a spy, the standard handling would have been to warn him immediately: "why wouldn't you go to him right away and tell him, hey, you have this problem. Don't talk to this person. Apparently, that didn't happen." He asked what national security secrets Huang supposedly leaked at all: "He doesn't work for the government. He's not, as far as I'm aware, privy to classified materials." He argued the IP China would want is not conveyed "over pillow talk" but is files that would allow tape-out of the next chip generation. Sacks is the first administration official in the record to argue on the record that a defensive briefing was the standard handling in the directly comparable Swalwell case and that its absence here is itself the anomaly. A second carriage of the same appearance, a long-form summary post read in full in the case record, carries a further Sacks line from the episode, that the only crime known for sure is the leaking of the classified memo that named Alice Huang; that line rests on the summary carriage, not on the transcript. THE STREET REPRICES THE OVERHANG • HSBC analyst Frank Lee downgraded Nvidia from Buy to Hold on Friday, November 13 and cut his price target to $170 from $365, saying the shares are likely to lag until a permanent succession plan is laid out and a new CEO demonstrates execution, and warning that tighter US export restrictions are a serious possibility. Per his note as reported by CNBC and carried by a market relay, about 11 percent of Nvidia's revenue over the last six quarters came from outside the US and Taiwan, and in his bear case losing that revenue would cut fiscal 2028 EPS by about 13 percent, to $13.57 from a $15.65 base case. The note was not read firsthand in the case record, and one secondary summary put the old target at $375 rather than $365; that detail is still settling. • Leo KoGuan, a billionaire Nvidia shareholder, told Bloomberg on Friday, November 13 that he will make no further investment in Nvidia without Jensen Huang, per Bloomberg's reporting carried identically across multiple carriages in the window; the Bloomberg original was not read firsthand in the case record. KoGuan says he has invested about $1.3 billion in Nvidia; that figure is his own and is not independently verified. He did not say he is selling the shares he holds: per the detailed carriage, he said nothing had changed about Nvidia's path, that he will cut planned investment rather than the shares he holds, and that he would add to SpaceX and Alphabet instead, or back Huang if Huang starts a company. He is the first named large shareholder in the record to state a concrete capital response to the exit, a pause on new buying tied expressly to Huang's absence. THE CHECKPOINTS • November 17: Nvidia earnings, and the Warren and Coons records preservation confirmation is due. • November 24: Bennet's answers due. • December 1: Huang's requested closed-door transcribed interview before the three House committees, and the House Foreign Affairs Democrats' answers due. • December 2: Teter's requested closed-door transcribed interview. • December 3: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Huang, and the Foreign Affairs hearing with Under Secretary Kessler at 10 a.m. • December 10: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Lutnick.

items.body: $NBIS $CRWV $DELL @MichaelDell said it best. Old GPUs are renting at a premium, and a HUGE premium at that. The H100 started shipping in 2022, and it now rents for 58% more than it did a year ago. That isn't how a depreciating asset is supposed to behave. This will keep happening as long as demand outruns supply. AI cloud providers that locked in long-term contracts at last year's prices are leaving money on the table right now. Those contracts roll off eventually, though, and when they do, that capacity gets repriced 50%+ higher on hardware that's already been running for years. The bear case for a GPU depreciating in 4 years is pretty much out of the picture now. I'll keep saying this to anyone who needs to hear it: forget the temporary price action. As long as demand and rental prices keep climbing, think long term, the way institutional players do. They keep accumulating at these prices because they don't care if we go lower next week. THEY KNOW we go higher in a year.

items.title: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE This is moronic. The China debate is a red herring. Set all of it aside. The spy question, the diversion question, whether Beijing even wants the chips. None
items.body: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE This is moronic. The China debate is a red herring. Set all of it aside. The spy question, the diversion question, whether Beijing even wants the chips. None of it decides whether Jensen Huang is fit to run a public company. What decides it: He carried on relationships with two subordinate employees, one of them a direct report. Every public company CEO knows that is disqualifying on its own. When questions did surface about the China issues, he did not disclose. He lied in writing to his own general counsel, Tim Teter, and his chief marketing officer, Alison Wagonfeld, telling them his dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed were "standard business dealings with customers." Reuters reports he gave similar assurances in the autumn of 2025, so the concealment ran for over a year. Only when the reporting closed in did he admit the unfaithfulness, in a November 8 email to staff. The board accepted his resignation on November 11. Intel forced out Brian Krzanich in 2018 for a consensual relationship with an employee. McDonald's fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 for the same and clawed back his severance. Neither case had a China angle. The relationship and the concealment were enough. No serious fiduciary would seat him again. CalPERS and the New York State Common Retirement Fund run withhold campaigns against directors for a fraction of this. The private market is clearer still. Apollo, Blackstone, Brookfield, Carlyle, and KKR would never let a portfolio company CEO survive this for a day. A sponsor-controlled board needs no campaign and no headlines. It makes one phone call. A CEO who will lie to his own general counsel to conceal a relationship with a direct report lacks the fiduciary fitness to run a public company. That conclusion requires no view on China at all. And the real opportunity here is to move on. Jensen played everyone for fools. The sooner that is accepted, the sooner Nvidia gets to grow and build again, quickly and strongly, as an institution instead of a one-man show. No choke points. No single point of failure. The company, and the AI industry built on top of it, comes out stronger for it.

items.title: I’ve been asked to comment on the “air pocket” bear narrative on $NVDA, which is getting louder. IMO, even in a stressed scenario the math doesn’t support a collapse. Hyperscalers
items.body: I’ve been asked to comment on the “air pocket” bear narrative on $NVDA, which is getting louder. IMO, even in a stressed scenario the math doesn’t support a collapse. Hyperscalers still make up roughly 50% of Data Center revenue. $MSFT, $AMZN, $GOOGL, $META and $ORCL have massive balance sheets and direct access to capital markets. They don’t need $NVDA’s financing to keep buying GPUs. That demand is real and largely independent of the circular deals. The part that actually depends on $NVDA’s balance sheet (equity stakes, guarantees, residual capacity) is much smaller. On the last earnings call, Kress said the labs they’re supporting should represent about 25% of the business next year. That’s the real “circular” exposure, not the whole company. It is real that the 25% is the high-growth piece (ACIE grew 138% year-over-year last quarter). If financing tightens (which I doubt will happen) and this segment slows, overall growth could decelerate from ~70% to ~40%. Painful for the multiple (is already a bit priced in), far from fatal for the business. So, as I see it: The “air pocket” is real. The size of the hole the bears are describing is not. I think $NVDA has a bright future that will be even brighter if Jensen comes back. At these levels, the stock price feels quite undervalued.

external_articles.title: SuperComputing (SC26)
external_articles.body:
At SC26, step inside the Vertiv booth and experience your current and future end-to-end data center infrastructure path.

Explore how power, cooling, infrastructure, services, and software work together to support increasingly complex AI and high-performance computing (HPC) environments.

Choose your path. Explore what’s possible with end-to-end systems and services built for multiple compute generations ahead.

As direct liquid cooling scales, the interface between IT systems and facility mechanical infrastructure becomes more critical. This BoF explores four challenges. First, high-temperature cooling (heat-reuse, IT thermal margins) and dew point (prevent condensation). Second, warm-water fluid quality (filtration and added chemicals to prevent corrosion, biological growth, and scaling). Third, temperature and fluid dynamics with rapid workload power swings (volumetric expansion, pump cavitation, facility response characteristics). Fourth, integrating telemetry into IT systems and building automation (predict thermal excursions, reduce trapped capacity). This session is intended for facility engineers, system integrators, operations, administrators, architects, and researchers in energy-efficiency and sustainability

Speaker: Chris Thompson, Vice President, Global Advanced Technology and Microgrid Solutions, Vertiv

Explore grid-to-rack power architecture considerations as rack densities advance toward 300 kW, 600 kW, and megawatt-class systems.

The session will compare AC, medium-voltage AC, 800 VDC, and centralized DC approaches while addressing storage, fault tolerance, load smoothing, grid interactivity, and GPU throttling risk.

From individual racks to the infrastructure supporting an entire AI environment, experience how Vertiv is connecting the pieces of the data center.

Explore how infrastructure choices vary by operational requirements and support the future direction of AI and HPC.

Come see the bigger picture at Booth 2028.

Planning an AI or HPC deployment, modernizing existing infrastructure, or preparing for higher rack densities?

Meet with a Vertiv specialist at SC26 to discuss your requirements and explore approaches for what’s next.

items.title: Power availability might be a bigger bottleneck for neoclouds than GPU supply. And $NBIS latest earnings call gave us a pretty good example of why. Back in August, Nebius learned t
items.body: Power availability might be a bigger bottleneck for neoclouds than GPU supply. And $NBIS latest earnings call gave us a pretty good example of why. Back in August, Nebius learned that its original plan to power the Vineland data center with diesel generators wasn’t going to work. The company switched to Bloom Energy’s fuel cells. The idea was to keep using temporary power supplied by DataOne while Bloom’s capacity gradually came online. But in late Q3, DataOne started winding down that temporary generation earlier than expected. Bloom wasn’t ready to cover the full demand yet. That left a gap in available power and pushed back parts of the deployment schedule. Arkady acknowledged that the switch cost Nebius a couple of months. Andrey Korolenko confirmed that Bloom is already generating electricity on-site, but the ramp-up is still ongoing. Importantly, the project didn’t stop. Nebius continued delivering capacity to Microsoft throughout Q3, with further deliveries planned for November and December. Now, why does this matter for the entire neocloud sector? Everyone is talking about secured gigawatts, GPU orders, and multibillion-dollar contracts. But there’s a lot that needs to happen between receiving those GPUs and actually billing customers for the capacity. You can have the building ready, thousands of GPUs installed, and a customer waiting to use them. Without enough reliable power, you can’t bring the next cluster online. And every month of delay can mean another month before you start recognizing revenue, even though much of the CapEx has already been spent. At this scale, the numbers get big very quickly. For some perspective, Nebius reported annual contract values above $25M per MW for deals signed in Q3. At that rate, a one-month delay in bringing 100 MW online represents roughly $208M in annual contract value allocated to that month. That’s not necessarily lost revenue. It could simply be pushed into a later period, depending on the contract terms. But it gives you an idea of how much money depends on getting the timing right. This is where behind-the-meter (BTM) power gets interesting. On-site generation is becoming an increasingly attractive option for data centers that can’t afford to wait years for grid connections. But BTM doesn’t magically solve the power problem. You still need fuel supply, electrical infrastructure, redundancy, and enough generation capacity to match the deployment schedule. And everything needs to work together. Vineland is a good example of how little room there is for error. If your temporary power source goes offline before the permanent solution is fully ramped up, your entire deployment schedule can slip. That’s also why I think Nebius handled the situation reasonably well. Bloom is already producing power, and Arkady mentioned that Nebius is considering using the technology at other sites. The new setup could even provide additional capacity at Vineland. We still don’t know exactly why the original diesel plan failed (@CABeyney it will great, if you can share us more details). But Nebius found an alternative and kept the project moving. Another interesting point from Arkady was his comment about third-party data center developments. He acknowledged that more things can go wrong when you’re relying on external developers. That’s one reason Nebius expects most of its new capacity in 2027 to come from its own sites, where it has more control over construction and deployment. I think investors will increasingly need to distinguish between companies that have secured power and those that can actually bring it online on schedule. Because having 1 GW in your pipeline is great. But it doesn’t tell you when that gigawatt will start making money.

items.title: I think TSMC’s planned investments in OpenAI and Anthropic could give it a clearer view of how much compute its customers ultimately need. Its board approved investments of up to $
items.body: I think TSMC’s planned investments in OpenAI and Anthropic could give it a clearer view of how much compute its customers ultimately need. Its board approved investments of up to $500 million in each company. One potential benefit is a more direct line to the AI developers whose demand feeds through cloud providers and chip designers into wafer orders. There’s this thing called the bullwhip effect in supply chains. When capacity is tight, companies can order extra to secure supply. If deployment plans later slip, each layer may cut those buffers. A modest change in end demand can then become a much larger drop in orders upstream. Thus, closer ties to the model developers could help $TSM compare their compute plans with the orders coming from chip customers, giving it another input when deciding how much capacity to build.

items.title: A lot of us are down significantly this year. I understand why people want to take a break and just hold on to their long-term positions. If you’re heavily invested in the AI secto
items.body: A lot of us are down significantly this year. I understand why people want to take a break and just hold on to their long-term positions. If you’re heavily invested in the AI sector then you’re probably down too because the whole sector has been hit over the past month or so. Anyone who has followed me from the beginning knows my portfolio has always been volatile. I knew that was going to be the case when I started investing because I wasn’t interested in the S&P 500 or ETFs. The difference now is the amount of money involved. When I had £10,000 invested, a 50% loss meant losing £5,000. That’s still a lot of money but it was something I could make back in a few months. Now that I have a six-figure portfolio, losing 50% would be a significant hit to my finances. Replacing that money through work could take me years. Throughout this year I’ve watched my portfolio move up and down by six figures. I like volatility and I like owning volatile stocks but I don’t like seeing swings of that size in both directions. This time it’s made me rethink how I manage my portfolio. I’m still a long-term investor and the majority of my money will always be in long-term holdings. I’m not panicking. My focus has always been on that part of my portfolio. With my short-term positions I usually cut losses quickly and move on. With my long-term holdings I’m willing to hold through volatility as long as I still believe in the business. Without going too deeply into it, there are three things I’m changing going forward. The first is that I won’t be going all in on one stock. At this point I can’t think of a scenario where I would be comfortable doing that again. I can have strong conviction in a company without letting it account for so much of my portfolio. The second is that I’ll be taking more profits and keeping some cash available. No stock goes up in a straight line and I don’t want to keep watching large gains disappear without taking anything off the table. Having cash also puts me in a better position to take advantage of sell-offs like this one. The third is that I’ll be looking at other sectors. I’ll still mainly invest in growth stocks but I want to diversify a little away from AI. It feels like almost any negative headline can trigger a sell-off across the sector right now. There’s already a lot of fear around AI and its impact on jobs, so I expect those headlines to keep coming. I don’t want so much of my portfolio reacting to the same news. I still want to grow my portfolio and I’m still comfortable taking risks. I just need to manage those risks better now that the amounts involved are much larger. If you’re also down significantly this year, I think it’s worth looking at your allocations, how much cash you keep and whether your approach still suits the amount you now have invested. We’re all going to make mistakes but we need to learn from them and make changes where we need to. NFA.

items.title: There is growing discussion that Jensen’s absence could actually accelerate the deflation of the AI bubble. Given how much NVIDIA has done to support financing across the AI ecosys
items.body: There is growing discussion that Jensen’s absence could actually accelerate the deflation of the AI bubble. Given how much NVIDIA has done to support financing across the AI ecosystem, I am starting to take this possibility more seriously. NVIDIA has helped expand the AI market by investing in AI companies and cloud providers, guaranteeing certain data center commitments, and agreeing to purchase unsold compute capacity. It has taken on some of its customers’ business risks so they could build more infrastructure. This circular financing structure has drawn plenty of criticism, but I believe it has played an important role in accelerating the industry’s expansion. NVIDIA committed capital and helped build infrastructure ahead of demand, giving models and services time to grow into that capacity. All of this rested on the conviction that future demand would be large enough. And Jensen was at the center of those bets. Now, the problem is.... who will be willing to keep taking that much risk to expand the market without Jensen? Arm CEO Rene Haas has been mentioned as a potential successor, but personally, I think even he would find it difficult to continue making the same kinds of bets. Beyond understanding the technology, he would have to convince the board and shareholders to put substantial company capital at risk for a future that has yet to materialize. I do not think a new CEO can immediately replicate the conviction and influence of a founder who spent decades proving his judgment through results. And this is not limited to future deals. Existing contracts can also be amended through renegotiation with the other parties. Publicly disclosed guarantee terms include provisions for amendments by written agreement, and some announced financing initiatives are still at the memorandum of understanding stage rather than final contracts. An announcement alone does not mean the full scale and execution timeline are locked in. What happens if the new leadership reviews existing investments and guarantees and imposes stricter conditions on additional support? Companies that built their investment plans around NVIDIA’s backing may have to revisit their financing assumptions. Even if projects are not canceled outright, smaller commitments or delayed spending could change the growth trajectory the market has been expecting. What concerns me is the potential chain reaction. If NVIDIA pulls back its support, lenders could demand more collateral or higher interest rates. That could reduce the amount of data center capacity companies can actually build, even if demand remains unchanged. Slower infrastructure expansion could then push back their growth and monetization timelines, making the next round of financing harder to secure. Personally, I currently see it as more likely that Jensen will not return. That makes me wonder whether I need to reassess my own view of the AI market. We need to consider how much of NVIDIA’s business its competitors could capture, but also whether the overall AI market can continue expanding at the pace we have been expecting. Even if demand for AI keeps growing, the market’s growth rate can change if fewer people are willing to believe in that future and take the risks needed to build it. How much of the AI future we have been anticipating depended on the assumption that Jensen would keep making the next big bet? I think that is something we now need to reconsider.

items.body: [Taiwan’s Weekly Standout #4] Taiwan Glass (1802 TT) reported a 56.5% jump in October revenue to NT$5.57 billion, citing stronger glass-fabric demand from AI and other smart technologies. Its shares rose 47.2% between the Nov. 6 and Nov. 13 closes. The company makes glass yarn and fabric used in electronic materials. Two product families connect it to AI hardware. Low-DK glass fabric helps reduce signal loss in high-speed circuit boards. Low-CTE glass fabric limits thermal expansion in chip-package substrates, helping reduce warping as the chip and substrate expand by different amounts when heated. We estimates that October revenue from high-end glass fabric rose about 14% to 17% from September. The two product families are ramping at different speeds. Low-CTE shipments began in small volumes in late 2025 and have increased substantially since early 2026. Low-DK2 is expected to contribute more revenue than Low-CTE in 2027, with Low-CTE narrowing the gap as new capacity comes online in the second half of 2027 and 2028. On Nov. 2, Chairman Lin Po-feng said high-end glass-fabric supply was still falling short of demand. Taiwan Glass is targeting 2027 completion and production for its third expansion phase and has launched a fourth, according to Economic Daily News. Our read is that Low-DK2 shipments for high-speed circuit boards matter more to near-term growth, while Low-CTE for package substrates offers a longer ramp.

external_articles.title: Singapore’s Investigations into Alice Huang (Huang Le) and Megaspeed International Pte Ltd
external_articles.body:
1. Singapore takes seriously its reputation as a trusted international trading and business hub. We uphold the rule of law and expect all companies operating in Singapore to conduct their business honestly and in accordance with our laws. While Singapore does not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, we expect all companies operating here to take into account such regulations, including export controls, in their international business activities. Singapore does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate other countries’ export controls through fraud or dishonest practices. Where there is evidence of breaches of Singapore law, we take firm action.

Singapore’s Investigations into Alice Huang and Megaspeed

2. In February 2025, the Singapore Police Force (“SPF”) and Singapore Customs initiated an independent investigation into several companies and their key officers, including Megaspeed International Pte Ltd (“Megaspeed”), a company incorporated in Singapore, and its controllers. The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences. As noted by Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs K Shanmugam at a press conference (opens in new tab) on 3 March 2025, Singapore’s investigations were not based on any request from any country or sovereign entity.

3. Alice Huang (otherwise known as Huang Le), a Hong Kong resident, was investigated for suspected involvement in the possible offences in Singapore, given her position as then-CEO, Chairperson, and one of the key controllers of Megaspeed. Huang was not based in Singapore, and was not investigated for espionage.

4. On 24 June 2025, the US Bureau of Industry and Security (“BIS”) conducted a voluntary Post-Shipment Verification (“PSV”) check at Megaspeed with Huang present. The PSV check was the first time Singapore came to know about the US’s interest in Megaspeed and Huang. On the same day, SPF also interviewed her as part of its ongoing investigations into Megaspeed. Her passport was impounded under Section 112 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 to secure her attendance for purposes of the ongoing investigations, since Huang was not based in Singapore.

5. The physical servers had been purchased by companies (which were under investigation) and exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the Singapore market. The SPF was investigating whether the servers had subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore. To establish the facts, SPF could not rely solely on declarations made by the companies in Singapore.  It also needed to verify these against information and records in other jurisdictions, including the jurisdictions from which the servers originated and their eventual destinations. Singapore therefore sought information from the US and other destination jurisdictions, to assist with our independent investigations.

6. In particular, the SPF sought information relating to Supermicro, a US-based supplier of servers, which was relevant to the SPF’s investigations. However, Supermicro provided limited cooperation. At a meeting on 7 July 2025, SPF and the Attorney-General’s Chambers (“AGC”) raised this issue with the US authorities and requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation. Since September 2025, SPF has repeated this request on several occasions to the US Department of Justice (“DOJ”) and the Federal Bureau of Investigations (“FBI”). Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company.

7. In February 2026, SPF, in consultation with AGC, concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.

8. However, SPF assessed that Huang had provided information which she knew to be inaccurate to SPF in the course of investigations, to downplay her role in Megaspeed. She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Other cases in the past have been dealt with in a similar way. SPF returned Huang’s passport on 26 February 2026, and she departed Singapore on the same day .

9. SPF’s investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing. None of the six persons have been in Singapore since investigations commenced in February 2025.

Firm Action Taken Against Entities that Violate Singapore’s Laws

10. Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices. Singapore has charged four individuals and four companies in Court between February 2025 and July 2026 for offences -- including fraud by false representation in relation to the purchase of servers, with the offences carrying imprisonment terms of up to 20 years each.

11. Our approach is clear. Singapore will conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it.

items.title: TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10AM TO 10PM on 11/13/26 Today the fight over the Megaspeed Entity List delay became an open cabinet split, the Commerce Secretary's own
items.body: TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10AM TO 10PM on 11/13/26 Today the fight over the Megaspeed Entity List delay became an open cabinet split, the Commerce Secretary's own tenure came into question, Reuters documented the scale of Chinese AI projects built around restricted Nvidia chips, and the succession search moved in public for the first time: the board was reported to have approached an external candidate, then issued its first statement calling candidate speculation premature, while two major holders asked the board to slow the process down and keep Jensen Huang's return on the table. The 8 p.m. deadline for Huang's written acceptance of the December 1 interview passed with nothing public. THE CABINET SPLIT GOES PUBLIC • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on the record on CNBC's Squawk Box this morning, in a quote verified verbatim from the program's video: "Treasury, War, USTR and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. But Commerce has the pen, Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to have to ask them about their internal processes." No cabinet secretary had previously stated the interagency split on the record, named the four agencies in favor, or assigned the failure to Commerce and BIS by name. • In the same interview, per Reuters' report of it, Bessent turned on Nvidia itself: "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" and "It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." He added that the authorities exist and "just need to be implemented," and that the FTC could possibly put something on its restrictive list alongside BIS. CNN's report of the same interview adds his frustration that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above A100s. • CNN reported today, per people familiar with the conversations, that some of President Trump's advisers have begun discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be dismissed over the Megaspeed failure, and that Trump has fielded calls from administration officials and outside advisers raising alarm about Lutnick. The White House statement of "complete confidence" in Lutnick was issued Thursday, before Bessent's public comments. This is CNN's reporting, a single source chain, not yet corroborated. THE CHANNEL, DOCUMENTED AT SCALE • Reuters reported today, from its review of more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, that Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia's restricted H100, H200 and H800 processors carry a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan, more than $3.2 billion. The figure is project value, including buildings, power systems and other infrastructure; it is not spending on Nvidia chips alone. Reuters states the figures do not establish how the restricted hardware reached Chinese users, that the projects have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang, and that there has been no public finding that Huang violated export-control laws. THE SUCCESSION SEARCH MOVES, THEN THE BOARD PUSHES BACK • The Financial Times reported today, per people familiar with the matter, that Nvidia's board has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas in its search for a permanent successor to Huang. Haas is one of several candidates under consideration; no offer has been made and there is no guarantee of one. The FT article is paywalled and its full text was not read firsthand by the case record; the details rest on the Reuters flash and full-summary carriages, which agree. Reuters could not independently verify the report, Arm declined to comment, and Nvidia gave no immediate response. Haas led Arm since February 2022 and previously spent about seven years at Nvidia, leaving in 2013. • Hours later, the board issued its first public statement on the search, telling CNBC: "We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role. We have not formally engaged any potential candidates." It added: "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature." The statement does not deny an approach: "formally engaged" is the operative qualifier, and it dates the process a day after the resignation took effect, with no search firm yet selected. • In the same CNBC report, per a person familiar with the matter, interim CEO Colette Kress conducted her first meeting as interim CEO on Thursday afternoon, November 12, with high-level executives at Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara. THE INTERIM CEO'S STANDING • The Wall Street Journal reported today, per a person familiar with the comments, that at a meeting this summer Huang summoned Kress and his senior finance team over Nvidia's ballooning chip-financing guarantees to companies that could not afford its chips, interrupted her presentation, and called her "a deer in the headlights" and a "reporting CFO" who could not help him define strategy or make decisions. • The Journal also reports that the credit-support program was led by Huang's son-in-law, VP Nico Caprez, that Kress behind the scenes tried to rein in Caprez, and that on the OpenAI Ohio campus backstop, a campus to be filled with about $300 billion of Nvidia chips, Kress reworked the deal and cut Nvidia's initial financial commitment in half, with the downsized deal signed on August 17. HOLDERS ASK THE BOARD TO SLOW DOWN • Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management sent a joint letter to Nvidia's board today, carried verbatim in full in the posts the case record read, asking the board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang," and warning against "a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders." The letter endorses the interim arrangement: "The company will be capably led in the interim by Colette Kress and team." It is the first intervention by holders of this weight, and it is holder pressure on the succession timeline, not a case fact. THE 8 P.M. DEADLINE • Huang's written acceptance of the December 1 closed-door transcribed interview was due by 8 p.m. EST today, or a subpoena would issue, under the three chairs' November 12 letter. The deadline passed with no public confirmation, refusal, subpoena issuance, or committee statement in the case record's coverage through about 10:16 p.m. EST, and nothing public on Teter's December 2 confirmation either. That is the public record only; a non-public delivery is not excluded. THE CHECKPOINTS • November 17: Nvidia earnings, and the Warren and Coons records preservation confirmation is due. • November 24: Bennet's answers due. • December 1: Huang's requested closed-door transcribed interview before the three House committees, and the House Foreign Affairs Democrats' answers due. • December 2: Teter's requested closed-door transcribed interview. • December 3: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Huang, and the Foreign Affairs hearing with Under Secretary Kessler at 10 a.m. • December 10: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Lutnick.
